Through his paintings, he not only preserves the legacy of Vietnamese lacquer painting but also redefines it, ensuring its relevance in the world of modern art.

provenance: Ben Thanh Art & Frame and Galerie Nguyen, HCMC, Vietnam. | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2013. | Private collection, Asia. | | Do Xuan Doan | 祭月 | 漆 木板 | 2006年作 | | 簽名：D X Doan 06（右下） | | 來源 | 越南胡志明市Ben Thanh Art & Frame 及 Nguyen藝廊 | 現藏家於2013年得自上述來源 | 亞洲私人收藏 | | | Do Xuan Doan, born in 1937, is a distinguished Vietnamese artist renowned for his contributions to modern and contemporary art. He graduated from the Hanoi College of Fine Arts in 1961 and developed a unique style that blends traditional Vietnamese themes with modern techniques. His formative years coincided with the Vietnam War, during which he joined the army, an experience that infused his artistic expression with resilience and social consciousness. | | Do Xuan Doan's paintings often illustrate scenes of rural life, capturing the harmony between man and nature. His works are characterised by vibrant colours, dynamic compositions, and the use of lacquer on wood, a traditional Vietnamese medium that adds depth and texture. His subjects include ancient houses, old streets, and ordinary people, where simplicity and sincerity are encapsulated. He enhances his paintings with a vibrant colour palette and bold brushstrokes. | | Defying the constraints of conventional categorisation, Do Xuan Doan seamlessly traverses the realms of realism, expressionism, surrealism, and abstraction. As one of the founders and leaders of the Young Artists Association in 1966, he played a pivotal role in encouraging innovation and experimentation among young artists, significantly influencing the development of modern Vietnamese art. | | Do Xuan Doan's contributions to Vietnamese culture and his role in shaping the Young Artists Association remain significant. His contemporary lacquer works continue to inspire and resonate with viewers, exemplifying creativity, resilience, and a commitment to pushing artistic boundaries. His enduring legacy reminds us of the power of expression and the beauty of capturing everyday life through visual art.

auction_title: Southeast Asian Modern and Contemporary Art
provenance: Acquired directly from the artist by the present owner in Vietnam in 2007. | Private collection, US. | | 鄧春和 | 生命循環 | 油彩 畫布 | 2007年作 | | 簽名：HOA 8/2007（左下） | | 此作經藝術家本人再認證 | | 來源 | 現藏家於2007年於越南直接得自藝術家本人 | 美國私人收藏 | | | Born in 1959, Dang Xuan Hoa occupies a central place in post-Doi Moi Vietnamese art. His work is distinguished by a visual language that combines the distilled clarity of folk art with the chromatic intensity of Post-Impressionist modernism. Rather than descriptive realism, his canvases are shaped by a search for emotional and symbolic resonance, with figures simplified to their essential forms and their presence conveyed through quiet gestures and finely drawn contours that recall the graphic precision of woodcuts or collage. Through self-portraits, family scenes and still lifes, Hoa weaves intimate narratives rooted in the rhythms of daily life. Yet his imagery consistently transcends the anecdotal. Ceramic vases, flowers, oil lamps, fruit bowls and cats recur as emblematic objects, functioning not as decoration, but as vessels of memory, identity and cultural inheritance. Through this interplay of human presence and a symbolic world of objects, Hoa constructs a pictorial universe that is both familiar and metaphysical, inviting viewers to look beneath the surface of the everyday. | | This large‑scale work belongs to Hoa's Life series, a period in which he shaped a more open and resonant visual language to explore the emotional, familial and spiritual threads that run through human experience. At the heart of this series is the fused grey couple, a recurring emblem that carries a quiet spiritual charge. Appearing across several works from the period, this elongated, merged figure gathers the idea of unity into a single, distilled form. Its muted colour and pared‑back outline strip away narrative detail, allowing it to stand as a constant presence within the series. It becomes an abstract expression of shared consciousness, mutual dependence and the cyclical nature of human bonds. | | In this painting, the grey union figure lies along the horizontal axis, giving the composition its quiet foundation. Rather than showing two bodies in contact, it appears as a single, continuous form, suggesting unity as an inner condition rather than an outward gesture. Its presence is calm and introspective, a still centre that lends the work its reflective, almost meditative atmosphere. | | Beside this emblematic couple stands a second composite figure, upright and two‑faced, one side male and the other female. If the grey couple functions as the spiritual emblem, this dual-gender figure operates as its physical incarnation, representing a more physical, earthly form. Its stance, its doubled face and its solid outline introduce a gentle contrast to the reclining stillness of the union figure. Together, the two forms evoke a dialogue between essence and appearance, inner life and outward presence, spiritual unity and the dualities of lived experience. | | A constellation of objects and small attendant figures unfolds around them, each rendered with the clarity of an emblem. Drawn from Hoa's long engagement with still life, these motifs act less as descriptive details than as traces of memory, domestic habit and cultural continuity. Their placement within the flattened space recalls the visual logic of folk painting and ancestral shrines, where objects and presences share the same plane without hierarchy. The painting's saturated fields of colour heighten this sense of symbolic stillness, setting the central forms against backgrounds that feel almost iconic. Here, colour is not used to describe the visible world but to set the emotional tone, giving the work its contemplative atmosphere. | | In bringing together these emblematic bodies, incarnated identities and symbolic objects, Hoa gives shape to the central concerns of his Life series: relational harmony, domestic interiority and the quiet metaphysics of everyday existence. The grey union figure, repeated across the series, serves as the spiritual emblem through which these themes are gathered, while the two‑faced vertical figure lends them physical presence. Together, they give the series its distinctive coherence and emotional depth.
subject_matter: couple, dual-gender figure, objects, flowers, ceramic vases, oil lamps, fruit bowls, cats

provenance: Acquired directly from the artist by the present owner in Vietnam in 2006. | Private collection, US. | | Nguyen Tu Nghiem | 扶董天王聖揀 | 設色紙本 | 1975年作 | | 簽名：nge 75（下） | | 來源 | 現藏家於2006年於越南直接得自藝術家本人 | 美國私人收藏 | | | Nguyen Tu Nghiem, born in Nghe An in north‑central Vietnam, trained at the École des Beaux‑Arts de l'Indochine from 1941 to 1945 and later continued his studies at the Vietnam Fine Arts College under To Ngoc Van during the Viet Bac years of 1946 and 1947. This early formation, shaped by both academic discipline and the cultural life of the resistance, laid the groundwork for one of the most distinctive artistic voices in modern Vietnamese painting. | | Working primarily in lacquer and gouache, he developed a highly individual style that moved beyond academic naturalism and drew deeply on the visual language of traditional Vietnamese art. Together with Bui Xuan Phai, Nguyen Sang and Duong Bích Lien, he is recognised as one of the four great masters of Vietnamese modern art, a group whose work helped define new artistic directions in the decades surrounding the period of Doi Moi. | | Nguyen Tu Nghiem's paintings reveal a sustained interest in the expressive potential of traditional motifs. His celebrated depictions of Thanh Giong and his recurring interpretations of the Vietnamese zodiac show how myth and symbolism could be reimagined through a modernist lens. Equally characteristic are his paintings of dancers, in which movement is distilled into rhythmic, stylised forms. These works evoke the energy of village festivals and ceremonial performance, yet they remain anchored in the structural clarity and abstraction of modern art. | | In 1996 he received the Ho Chí Minh Prize for Literature and the Arts, a recognition of his lasting contribution to Vietnam's cultural heritage.

auction_title: Southeast Asian Modern and Contemporary Art
provenance: Acquired directly from the artist by the present owner in Vietnam in 2007. | Private collection, US. | | Dinh Y Nhi | 安檢 | 油彩 畫布 | 2007年作 | | 簽名：Nhi 2007（左下） | | 來源 | 現藏家於2007年於越南直接得自藝術家本人 | 美國私人收藏 | | | Dinh Y Nhi (born Hanoi, 1967) is one of the few women artists to have made a significant impact on Vietnam's art scene in the early 1990s, a period still shaped by male dominance and by the expectation that women artists should remain within decorative or traditionally 'feminine' modes of expression. Her refusal to be defined by these expectations has shaped her entire career. From the outset, she positioned herself against aesthetic softness and narrative comfort, instead developing a language of psychological tension, minimal figuration and emotional directness. This stance established her as an important and occasionally disruptive presence within a rapidly shifting cultural landscape. | | From the early 2000s, Dinh Y Nhi extends her commitment to minimal figuration of her early years into a more expressive, psychologically charged idiom, using colour, distortion, and textual fragments to articulate the pressures of contemporary Vietnamese life. Her figures rarely settle into stable identities. They twist, stretch, or lean forward as if caught between self‑assertion and exposure, their expressions hovering in a state of unresolved tension. Colour is introduced more fully in her later practice. It functions not as embellishment but as atmosphere. Reds, ochres, and dense blacks create emotional climates. In these climates the figures appear to struggle for equilibrium. | | Security Checked (2007) is a prime example of this mature phase. Three distorted figures occupy the foreground, their limbs extended and their hollow eyes fixed in an uneasy state of awareness. The vivid, layered and agitated red background heightens the sense of psychological heat. The phrase 'SECURITY CHECKED' appears in uneven strokes across the lower register. Instead of talking about a real checkpoint, it brings to mind the feeling of being judged in all sorts of ways, socially, institutionally or emotionally, in a society that's figuring out new ways of moving and being regulated. The text acts as atmospheric pressure rather than narrative cue, reinforcing the idea that the figures are caught in a moment of inspection. | | The painting's power lies in its refusal of specificity. These are not individuals undergoing a particular event; they are embodiments of a broader condition, suspended between autonomy and external judgement. This approach allows Security Checked to distil the concerns that run through Nhi's practice. These concerns include the instability of identity, the tension between visibility and vulnerability, and the quiet violence of being measured. The work also highlights her importance as one of the few women artists of her generation to express such themes with such clarity.
subject_matter: three figures, distorted limbs, hollow eyes, red background, text 'SECURITY CHECKED', emotional tension, instability of identity, vulnerability, social judgement, psychological heat

artwork_title: Interior Scene with Two Balinese Women
provenance: Collection of Dr and Mrs B.S. Tio. Acquired directly from the artist in Indonesia prior to 1948. | Thence in the family by descent. | Private collection, the Netherlands. | | 勒邁耶 | 室內 | 油彩 畫布 配原裝巴厘手工雕刻畫框 | 約1948年作 | | 簽名：J. Le Mayeur（左下） | | 來源 | B.S. Tio 醫生伉儷珍藏，其於1948年以前於印尼直接得自藝術家本人 | 後經家族流傳至今 | 荷蘭私人收藏 | | 註：本作附藝術家原裝巴厘手工畫框 | | 本作品附《勒邁耶：藝術家及旅遊家》作者Jop Ubbens博士開立之作品保證書。此作品亦將納入荷蘭布瑟姆勒邁耶文獻庫（LMA） | | | This beautiful painting, Interior Scene with Two Balinese Women, belonged to Dr B.S. Tio (1909-1986) and his wife Djoenariah Kadjat. Dr Tio was born into a long‑established Chinese merchant family in Central Java in Indonesia. He trained in medicine at the Dutch East Indies Medical School (NIAS) in Surabaya, and after receiving his medical degree he served in a series of medical appointments across the archipelago. | | In early 1948, they moved to the Netherlands, where Dr Tio undertook further specialisation in dermato‑venereology at the Department of Skin and Venereal Diseases of the Binnengasthuis in Amsterdam. While Djoenariah Kadjat and their kids remained in the Netherlands, Dr Tio was invited by the Indonesian government to return to Bandung, where he worked between 1949 and 1963. He settled permanently in the Netherlands in 1963, continuing his career as a dermato‑venereologist. | | According to the family, the painting was acquired by Dr and Mrs Tio shortly before their departure for the Netherlands in 1948. | | Adrien‑Jean Le Mayeur de Merprès first arrived in Bali in 1932 and was immediately captivated by the island's radiance, the cadence of its ceremonies, and above all the elegance and natural poise of Balinese women. These encounters shaped the remainder of his career. His paintings fuse European Impressionist sensibility with Balinese visual culture, creating a body of work in which light, colour, and daily ritual are rendered with an intimate, lived immediacy. | | In 1935 he married the young legong dancer Ni Polok, who became his muse and the central figure in many of his compositions. After their marriage he transformed their house in Sanur into a richly decorated residence, studio, and gallery. At that time Sanur was still a quiet fishing village, and the house, filled with carved wood, patterned textiles, stone sculpture, and abundant flowers, became the heart of his artistic world. Ni Polok continued to live there after the artist's death until her own passing in 1985, and the property is now preserved as the Le Mayeur Museum. | | The present painting, Interior Scene with Two Balinese Women (circa 1948), is one of a small number of works that depict the interior of the Sanur house. Two women occupy the centre of the composition. One stands while the other crouches to arrange flowers on a low table. Their gestures are calm and deliberate, and the surrounding space is filled with Balinese architectural and decorative elements. Carved pillars, red terrazzo tiles, stone figures, and patterned fabrics come together to create an intimate yet ceremonial setting. | | A comparison with the painting Two Women Arranging Flowers in the Interior (circa 1950), sold at Bonhams Hong Kong, 22 April 2021, lot 36 (Fig. 2), is particularly revealing. Both works are viewed from a similar angle and share the same underlying structure, including the positioning of the two large paintings at the back of the room. However, the details differ between the two canvases. The shape of the table, the small objects, and the decorative accents vary subtly. A recent photograph of the house taken from the same viewpoint confirms the architectural framework common to both paintings. This enables us to gain insight into how Le Mayeur worked. Rather than recording the room with strict documentary accuracy, he adjusted and refined its elements to create a harmonious composition. He captured the essence of his surroundings without getting bogged down in unnecessary detail. | | Le Mayeur's training in Impressionism is evident throughout his work. His deepest interest lies in the interplay of light and colour, in capturing the warmth of the tropics and the fleeting sensation of a moment held still. This approach becomes clear when comparing the two interior scenes. The painting sold in our Hong Kong saleroom in 2021 carries a cooler daylight clarity, while the present work is enveloped in a richer orange brown glow that suggests late afternoon light filtering through the house. As Robert Pelfrey wrote of Monet, 'The subjects did not change, but the visual sensations... changed constantly'. Le Mayeur's interiors resonate with this idea: the constancy of place becomes a stage for endlessly shifting atmospheres. | | The painting retains its original carved wooden frame, crafted by the carpenter who worked in Le Mayeur's household. Frame and canvas together form a unified object that reflects the artist's domestic world and his deep engagement with Balinese craftsmanship. The work stands as a finely balanced evocation of the artist's home, an intimate and ornamentally rich space that shaped his vision and remains central to an understanding of his mature style.
subject_matter: interior, two Balinese women, flowers, low table, carved pillars, red terrazzo tiles, stone figures, patterned fabrics, Balinese architecture, domestic space

auction_title: Southeast Asian Modern and Contemporary Art
provenance: Private collection, US. | | Do Quang Em | 裸像 | 油彩 畫布 | 1974年作 | | 簽名：DOQUANGEM 74（左上）簽名、地點、畫題及紀年（背） | | 來源 | 美國私人收藏 | | | Do Quang Em was born in 1942 in the quiet province of Ninh Thuan in Vietnam and trained at the Gia Dinh College of Fine Arts in Saigon, graduating in 1965. He co-founded the Young Saigonese Artists Association the following year and later returned to Gia Dinh as a professor in 1973 and 1974, becoming an influential presence in the artistic life of southern Vietnam. His work is admired for its clarity and refinement, with a realist style that recalls the light and depth of Caravaggio and Rembrandt and the quiet precision of the Dutch masters. Realism was not widely practised among southern Vietnamese artists of his generation, which makes his approach distinctive and immediately recognisable. | | He is best known for his still lifes featuring teapots and cups, as well as his intimate portraits of women, often his wife and daughter. However, the present work Nude – Miss Kim Ngân stands apart as a rare nude within his oeuvre. Painted in 1974 during his tenure as a professor at Gia Dinh, and only a year before the Fall of Saigon, a pivotal moment in Vietnamese history. The Fall of Saigon in April 1975 marked the end of the Vietnam War and the collapse of the South Vietnamese government, bringing profound social and political change to the country. The painting was created at a time when political uncertainty lent a particular intensity to scenes of private domestic life. | | The sitter lies across a bed of white sheets, her body arranged in a natural diagonal that guides the eye from her raised arm to the gentle curve of her legs. Her torso turns slightly, allowing the light to shape the chest and abdomen with soft transitions of tone. One arm rests behind her head, the other falls loosely at her side, and her gaze drifts forward, absorbed in thought. Light enters from the upper left, warming the throat and shoulders while the far side of the body settles into a quieter shadow. Small touches, such as the faint gleam on her fingernails, add a note of quiet elegance without disturbing the calm of the scene. | | The painting brings together the qualities that define Do Quang Em's finest work, from his sensitive handling of light to his ability to give everyday interiors a sense of stillness and dignity. As a rare nude from an important early period, it offers a compelling insight into the artist's development and his enduring interest in the quiet poetry of the human figure. The title Miss Kim Ngân Number 5 is written in the artist's own hand on the reverse, indicating that this work forms part of a small and seldom seen series devoted to the same sitter.
subject_matter: nude, woman, bed, white sheets, light, shadow, raised arm, curve of legs, torso, domestic interior

provenance: Collection of Helen & Lewis Jongeneel, US. Acquired in the Philippines during Lewis Jongeneel's assignment there to assist in establishing a Del Monte pineapple processing facility. | Thence in the family by descent. | Private collection, US. | | 阿莫索羅 | 在稻田裡 | 油彩 畫布 | 1931年作 | | 簽名：F. Amorsolo MANILA 1931（左下） | | 來源 | 美國 Helen及Lewis Jongeneel伉儷珍藏 | Lewis Jongeneel 奉派前往菲律賓協助建立德爾蒙特（Del Monte）鳳梨加工廠期間得自當地 | 後經家族流傳至今 | 美國私人收藏 | | | This painting was acquired by the grandparents of the present owner, whose family owned the Del Monte pineapple enterprise. Founded in Hawaii in the late nineteenth century as a modest agricultural venture, the company soon expanded into a significant global operation. From the 1920s onward, Lewis Jongeneel travelled frequently to the Philippines to help establish a factory for the company. During these stays, he trained local communities in successful pineapple cultivation. He later carried out similar work in Haiti and eventually returned to the Philippines, where he passed away. | | It was during one of his assignments in the Philippines that he acquired this painting, which has remained in the family across generations. | | The scene unfolds gradually, inviting the viewer to move from the quiet coolness of the periphery into the sunlit heart of the composition. The darker and cooler tones of the bamboo grove on the left form a natural boundary, while the shaded earth and reflective water across the lower part of the painting create a calm horizontal band that anchors the landscape and evokes the fertility and cyclical renewal of rice cultivation. These cooler passages—found in the bamboo grove, the shaded foreground, and the distant mountain—recede into the distance, creating a gentle perimeter that prepares the viewer for what lies at the centre. | | As the gaze moves naturally along this visual pathway, the warmer and brighter heart of the painting reveals itself. Here, the cluster of workers in the rice field, together with the man riding the carabao, occupies the central place in the composition. This is where the narrative, movement, and human presence converge. Their prominence is heightened by the artist's use of warm yellows and ochres, which advance towards the viewer, while the surrounding cooler greens and blues of the bamboo grove, the shaded foreground, and the distant mountain fade into the background. By distributing the major elements across the scene and concentrating chromatic intensity around the focal group, the artist creates a composition that is both dynamic and coherent, guiding the viewer effortlessly towards the central activity. | | This arrangement has an equally resonant iconographic intention. The bamboo represents a guardian of the rural world, while the reflective water symbolises fertility and the cyclical nature of agricultural life. The workers and the carabao form an emblem of communal labour and agrarian identity, their placement within this balanced composition suggesting an ordered and idealised relationship with nature. The interplay of warm and cool tones, the gentle framing by landscape elements, and the luminous depiction of rural labour are characteristic of Amorsolo's mature style. Through these choices, the painting offers a vision of the Philippines as a harmonious and abundant land, rooted in a timeless agricultural tradition.

provenance: Collection of Mr. Hugo von Platen Luder (1889-1957), US, acquired in Manila circa 1947. | Thence in the family by descent. | Private collection, US. | | 阿莫索羅 | 在芒果樹下煮飯 | 油彩 畫布 | 1947年作 | | 簽名：F. Amorsolo MANILLA 1947（左下） | | 來源 | 美國Hugo von Platen Luder先生舊藏，於1947年間得自馬尼拉 | 後經家族流傳 | 美國私人收藏 | | | This painting was acquired in Manila directly from the artist by Hugo von Platen Luder (1889–1957), the grandfather of the present owner, shortly after the end of the Second World War. As an entrepreneur, he travelled regularly to the Philippines for business during the 1940s and developed a particular admiration for Fernando Amorsolo's work in the post‑war years. It was during one of these visits that he obtained the present piece, which has remained in the von Platen Luder family ever since, passing through successive generations. | | Cooking Under the Mango Tree is among Amorsolo's most recognisable rural compositions, and several versions of the subject are known. This 1947 example captures an intimate moment of domestic respite beneath the broad, sheltering canopy of a mango tree, its foliage filtering the tropical light into the warm, golden radiance characteristic of the artist's mature style. Beneath its shade, a woman tends a clay stove, while nearby a mother sits with her child, the child's gaze extending toward the father who stands just beyond. A tethered carabao rests in the background, suggesting a pause from the labour of the surrounding fields. | | The interplay of light and shade is central to the composition: the cool shelter of the tree contrasts with the sunlit landscape beyond, allowing Amorsolo to demonstrate his mastery of dappled light as it falls across the figures and the earth. The scene highlights the close relationship between family, work, and community, capturing everyday life with the clarity of form, careful modelling, and luminous atmosphere that define his art. | | Amorsolo's reputation rose dramatically in the years following the war, and he became one of the most sought‑after artists in Manila. Collectors, returning residents, and foreign visitors frequently requested scenes that evoked rural life, domestic harmony, and the resilience of Filipino traditions. In response to this demand, Amorsolo adopted a more efficient working method, relying on established compositional structures, such as shaded tree canopies, central female figures, and arrangements of domestic activities, which he adapted for individual patrons by varying figures, gestures, utensils, or landscape details. This approach enabled him to meet the volume of commissions while preserving the distinctive qualities of light, atmosphere, and craftsmanship that define his work.

provenance: Acquired in Singapore in the late 1960s by the grandfather of the present owner. | Thence in the family by descent. | Private collection, US | | 鍾泗濱 | 母與子 | 油彩 畫布 | 1965年作 | | 簽名: 亖賓（右）、SOO PIENG 65（背） | | 來源 | 現藏家外祖父於1960年代晚期得自新加坡 | 後經家族流傳至今 | 美國私人收藏 | | | Created two years after Cheong Soo Pieng's return from a formative European tour, Maternity (1965) is a quiet, intimate scene. The minimal background, painted in muted earth tones, draws the viewer's attention to the figures. A mother sits calmly and steadily on the floor beside a cradle, while the child lies peacefully beside her, suggesting a moment of maternal care and serenity. | | The subject of motherhood has long occupied a central place in Western art. From sacred Renaissance art depicting the Madonna and Child to the tender domestic scenes of Mary Cassatt in the 19th century, motherhood has been portrayed as both divine and deeply human. Such works frequently emphasise the emotional bond between mother and child through composition, gesture and gaze, conveying intimacy and care. While Maternity resonates with this tradition, the artist's eclectic approach expresses a Southeast Asian sensibility. | | The delineation of elongated limbs and figures with simplified forms, reminiscent of wayang kulit (shadow puppets), is a hallmark of Soo Pieng's oeuvre. The red pendant around the mother's neck, known as buah kabo, is native to the Dayaks in Borneo. The formal elements of this painting are further enriched by Soo Pieng's exposure to European modernism. The influence of Amedeo Modigliani is evident: the slender, elongated body of the mother and her almond-shaped eyes recall Modigliani's portraits. However, the woman's face is deliberately obscured, which universalises the subject and shifts the viewer's focus to the symbolic and compositional elements rather than to individual identity. | | In this vein, Maternity becomes a site of cultural synthesis, where East and West, tradition and innovation converge. It not only offers a meditation on motherhood but also combines Southeast Asian cultural themes with modernist aesthetics, demonstrating a masterful expression of Soo Pieng's mature Nanyang Style.

Following his migration to Singapore with his father, he refined his artistic abilities. Subsequently, in 1932, he relocated to Jakarta, Indonesia, where he became involved in the local art scene. His opposition to Japanese colonialism during World War II resulted in his imprisonment. However, he was released through the intervention of a Japanese officer who recognised his artistic potential. | | Lee Man Fong was awarded a Malino Scholarship, which enabled him to pursue his studies in the Netherlands for a period of three years. Following the success of his European exhibitions, he returned to Indonesia before holding shows across Europe. His exceptional works were aligned with President Sukarno's taste, resulting in his appointment as the next presidential painter. His art, characterised by a unique visual language, made a significant contribution to postcolonial Southeast Asian art, resonating with viewers and capturing the essence of the region's landscapes and culture.

Cheong Soo Pieng was born in Xiamen, China, in 1917. He relocated to Singapore in 1946, where he found a creative environment that was both culturally rich and vibrant. This relocation marked the beginning of his search for a locally-focused artistic identity and new forms of expression. | | Over the course of his forty-year career, Cheong Soo Pieng demonstrated a commitment to exploring a diverse range of mediums and techniques. His early works, rooted in the Nanyang art style, vividly depicted the vibrancy of Southeast Asia. However, his venture into abstraction proved to be a defining moment in his career. His meticulous painting techniques and evolving personal style had a significant impact on the development of early contemporary art in Singapore. | | Cheong Soo Pieng's extensive travels across Southeast Asia and Europe provided him with invaluable experience and insight, enabling him to incorporate a diverse range of aesthetic elements into his work. A significant turning point was his 1952 trip to Bali with fellow artists Chen Chong Swee, Chen Wen Hsi, and Liu Kang. This trip helped establish the unique Nanyang style, which became a cornerstone of Singapore's modern art movement. | | Cheong Soo Pieng's unwavering dedication to artistic exploration and mastery of diverse techniques had a profound and enduring impact. His pioneering spirit continues to inspire new generations of artists, cementing his status as a seminal figure in Singapore and Southeast Asia's art history. Despite his passing in 1983, Cheong Soo Pieng's legacy continues to flourish.

He graduated from the Hanoi College of Fine Arts in 1961 and developed a unique style that blends traditional Vietnamese themes with modern techniques. His formative years coincided with the Vietnam War, during which he joined the army, an experience that infused his artistic expression with resilience and social consciousness. | | Do Xuan Doan's paintings often illustrate scenes of rural life, capturing the harmony between man and nature. His works are characterised by vibrant colours, dynamic compositions, and the use of lacquer on wood, a traditional Vietnamese medium that adds depth and texture. His subjects include ancient houses, old streets, and ordinary people, where simplicity and sincerity are encapsulated. He enhances his paintings with a vibrant colour palette and bold brushstrokes. | | Defying the constraints of conventional categorisation, Do Xuan Doan seamlessly traverses the realms of realism, expressionism, surrealism, and abstraction. As one of the founders and leaders of the Young Artists Association in 1966, he played a pivotal role in encouraging innovation and experimentation among young artists, significantly influencing the development of modern Vietnamese art. | | Do Xuan Doan's contributions to Vietnamese culture and his role in shaping the Young Artists Association remain significant. His contemporary lacquer works continue to inspire and resonate with viewers, exemplifying creativity, resilience, and a commitment to pushing artistic boundaries. His enduring legacy reminds us of the power of expression and the beauty of capturing everyday life through visual art.
